reference.source: Paediatric endocrinology and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by SRD5A2 variants that impair conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone.
Neonates have undervirilised or ambiguous external genitalia (perineoscrotal hypospadias, micropenis, bifid scrotum and a blind-ending vaginal pouch) and many are initially assigned female.
Testosterone-dependent Wolffian structures (epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles) are present and Müllerian structures are absent, with testes often in the inguinal canal or labioscrotal folds.
Marked virilisation occurs at puberty (the basis of the colloquial 'guevedoces'), with phallic growth, voice deepening and increased muscle bulk.
Dihydrotestosterone-dependent features remain limited: little prostatic growth, sparse beard, and absence of temporal balding and acne.
A raised testosterone-to-dihydrotestosterone ratio, at baseline or after human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation, supports the diagnosis, confirmed by SRD5A2 sequencing.
Gynaecomastia is characteristically absent, distinguishing it from androgen insensitivity, and libido and erectile function typically develop.
Many individuals raised female adopt a male gender identity around puberty, so early multidisciplinary counselling on sex of rearing is essential.
reference.pathophysiology: Steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency is an autosomal recessive 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SRD5A2, which encodes the type 2 isozyme that converts testosterone to the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone. Dihydrotestosterone is essential for virilisation of the external genitalia, urogenital sinus and prostate during intrauterine development, whereas the testosterone-dependent Wolffian derivatives (epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles) form normally and Müllerian structures regress under the influence of intact anti-Müllerian hormone from Sertoli cells. Affected individuals are therefore born with undervirilised or ambiguous external genitalia but normal internal male ducts and testes. At puberty the rise in testosterone, together with residual dihydrotestosterone generated by the type 1 isozyme, drives substantial virilisation, yet dihydrotestosterone-dependent features such as prostatic growth, terminal facial and body hair, temporal recession and acne remain deficient. A raised testosterone-to-dihydrotestosterone ratio, especially after human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation, is characteristic.
additionalDifferentials: Defects of testosterone biosynthesis such as 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase or 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency
Isolated hypospadias or micropenis of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype confirming 46,XY, with rapid sex-chromosome FISH if needed
Serum testosterone and dihydrotestosterone with calculation of their ratio, including a human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation test
Luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, and anti-Müllerian hormone or inhibin B
Pelvic and inguinal ultrasound with genitography to define internal anatomy and confirm absent Müllerian structures
Urinary steroid metabolite profile (5-alpha to 5-beta ratio) by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry
Assessment of gonadal position, with histology if clinically indicated
redFlags: Ambiguous genitalia in a neonate, which is a medical and social urgency requiring specialist disorder-of-sex-development referral
Salt-losing or adrenal features, which point instead to congenital adrenal hyperplasia and a risk of adrenal crisis
Undescended or intra-abdominal testes with their attendant longer-term malignancy considerations
Psychological distress relating to gender identity and sex of rearing
Delayed diagnosis leading to inappropriate irreversible genital surgery
reference.prognosis: With timely diagnosis, careful decisions about sex of rearing and multidisciplinary support the outlook is good; spontaneous virilisation occurs at puberty, although fertility is usually impaired and ongoing psychosocial support is important.
pitfalls: Assigning female sex of rearing and undertaking early irreversible genital surgery before the diagnosis and the likelihood of pubertal virilisation are appreciated
Being misled by a normal or only mildly raised testosterone-to-dihydrotestosterone ratio in infancy, when stimulation testing or genetic analysis may be required
Confusing it with androgen insensitivity, in which gynaecomastia occurs and pubertal virilisation does not
Overlooking the type 1 isozyme contribution that explains virilisation at puberty
Missing cryptorchidism and neglecting gonadal surveillance
references: Consensus statements on the management of disorders of sex development
Clinical genetics references on 46,XY disorders of sex development
management: Multidisciplinary decision on sex of rearing after diagnosis, recognising that marked spontaneous virilisation occurs at puberty and that some individuals later change gender.

Topical or systemic dihydrotestosterone to enhance phallic growth, or testosterone, when a male sex of rearing is chosen, with oestrogen replacement and gonadectomy considered where a female path is pursued.
Careful timing of any genital surgery such as hypospadias repair or orchidopexy for undescended testes, deferring irreversible elective procedures.
Ongoing psychosocial support for the individual and family through childhood and adolescence.
Surveillance of pubertal development, virilisation and gonadal position.
Fertility counselling, as fertility is usually impaired.
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive SRD5A2 disorder, with confirmatory testing and family screening.
